meta.description: Not Covey’s wording. The ladder warning was newspaper filler in 1915, tentatively credited to Allen Raine. Covey popularized it from 1986.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You may climb the ladder of success only to find it is leaning against the wrong wall'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Covey’s wording. The warning was in print in 1915, seventeen years before he was born. Quote Investigator credits Allen Raine — tentatively.

answer.label: Not Covey’s wording — in print since 1915
answer.authorDates: 1836–1908 · Welsh novelist · credited only tentatively, by Quote Investigator
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traces the saying to a boxed filler item in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 30 December 1915, signed “Allen Raine” — and credits her only tentatively ↗, noting that “Allen Raine” was the pen name of the Welsh novelist Anne Adalisa Evans but that it cannot be certain the newspaper meant her. Stephen Covey was using the metaphor by 1986 and made it famous in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, yet his own sentence runs “work harder and harder at climbing the ladder of success only to discover it’s leaning against the wrong wall” — the smooth “You may climb…” version circulating today is closest to a Los Angeles Times reporter’s 1986 rendering of his spoken talk, not to anything printed on his page.

source.excerpt: You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall.—Allen Raine.
trail: The earliest evidence is not a book but newspaper filler: Quote Investigator’s footnote ↗ gives The Brooklyn Daily Eagle, 30 December 1915, Picture and Sporting section, quote page 4, column 6 — a boxed item reading “You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall.—Allen Raine.”

The saying then drifts for two generations, its credit fading. QI logs printings ↗ in which a Marysville, Ohio paper still signs it “—A. Raine.” in 1950, but the Danville, Virginia and Boston Daily Globe printings of 1954 and Evan Esar’s 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968 carry no attribution at all, and by 1972 the Chicago Tribune credits a “Mae Maloo” — a name we have not been able to trace, and one QI prints without comment.

Covey enters late. QI documents the Los Angeles Times reporting in 1986 ↗ that he used the metaphor in his business lectures, and then his own sentence in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People — which is where the “ladder of success” phrasing attaches for good.

The line Covey is actually on record for is a different, sharper one. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ gives, from The Seven Habits Of Highly Effective People (1989) at page 101, his contrast between management as efficiency in climbing the ladder and leadership as determining whether the ladder leans against the right wall.
source.excerptNote: Note what is missing from the 1915 form: no “success,” no “wrong wall.” Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the wording drifting for decades — “wrong wall” is in print by 1954, and “the ladder of success” arrives with Covey in the 1980s. One bibliographic caution, offered for transparency: QI’s footnote cites Covey’s book as 1988 at quote page 98, while Wikipedia ↗ and Open Library both give first publication as 1989. That is an edition or printing difference and does not touch the origin story.

source.rightsNote: The wording people actually circulate descends from Covey: his sentence in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, first published in 1989 by Free Press ↗, and the 1986 Los Angeles Times report of his talks. Both are well after 1930, so both remain in copyright in the United States. The 1915 Brooklyn Daily Eagle sentence quoted above is a different and much older wording, and it is long in the public domain — if you need an unencumbered version of the thought, quote that one.

author.name: Allen Raine
author.heading: Who was Allen Raine?
author.metaLine: 1836–1908 · Welsh novelist · pen name of Anne Adalisa Beynon Puddicombe, née Evans
author.bio: “Allen Raine” was the pen name of a Welsh novelist born at Newcastle Emlyn in 1836, whose stories of coastal Cardiganshire were enormous sellers — more than two million copies by 1912 ↗. She took the National Eisteddfod prize in 1894, and novels including Torn Sails and By Berwen Banks were adapted for early film. The credit here is tentative, and one detail should keep it that way: she died in 1908, so the 1915 newspaper filler signed with her pen name appeared seven years after her death. That is our own observation, not Quote Investigator’s — its stated doubt is narrower: it simply cannot confirm the paper meant this Allen Raine. (We follow Wikipedia in spelling her middle name Adalisa; Quote Investigator spells it Adaliza.)

copyAttribution: Not Stephen Covey's wording. The saying was already in print in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 30 December 1915 as “You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall.—Allen Raine.” Quote Investigator tentatively credits Allen Raine, the pen name of Welsh novelist Anne Adalisa Evans (1836–1908), while noting the credit cannot be confirmed. Stephen Covey popularized the saying from 1986 and in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), but his own sentence differs from the version usually quoted.

misattribution.heading: What the credit gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The warning itself is genuine and Covey genuinely used it. Almost every credit attached to it is still wrong in some way — about the words, about the idea, or about the person.

items.why: Covey used the metaphor, but not in these words. QI quotes his book sentence ↗ as beginning “work harder and harder at climbing the ladder of success…” and the 1986 Los Angeles Times rendering as “they may climb the ladder of success only to find it’s leaning against the wrong wall.” The familiar “You may climb…” is a smoothing of the reporter’s sentence.

It was in print in December 1915, seventeen years before Covey was born in 1932, and QI tracks it through 1950, 1954, 1968 and 1972 printings ↗ before he ever used it. Covey popularized the saying; he did not coin it.
QI eliminates him ↗: Merton was born in 1915, the same year as the earliest citation, and QI reports finding no substantive evidence linking the notion to him.

“As you climb the ladder of success, be sure it’s leaning against the right building” appears in Brown’s P.S. I Love You (1990), which Wikipedia describes as a collection of his mother’s sayings and observations ↗ rather than his own; QI’s conclusion names Sarah Frances Brown as a popularizer of the saying.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest version anyone has located is a boxed filler item in The Brooklyn Daily Eagle of 30 December 1915, signed “Allen Raine” — and Quote Investigator credits her only tentatively ↗, because it cannot confirm the paper meant the Welsh novelist who wrote under that name. Our own note: she died in 1908 ↗, seven years before the filler ran.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Covey
lead: The line survives because it does a job no single word does: it separates being effective from being right. Covey built a real distinction on exactly that — in The Seven Habits at page 101 ↗ he casts management as efficiency in climbing the ladder and leadership as deciding which wall it leans against. The book had sold more than twenty million copies by the time he died in 2012 ↗, and the metaphor belongs to him in the popular mind whether or not he wrote the sentence being quoted.

But the joke is older than the management theory, and for decades it had no owner at all. It moved as newspaper filler, reshaped at every retelling: a Danville, Virginia paper in 1954 had someone reach the top and discover the ladder was against the wrong wall, and in 1972 the Chicago Tribune ran a version credited to a “Mae Maloo” who is, as far as we can tell, otherwise untraceable — Quote Investigator prints the item without comment ↗.
detailsBody: 1915 — the ladder, no success, no wrong wall. “You may get to the very top of the ladder, and then find it has not been leaning against the right wall.” The failure is framed positively: the wall was simply not the right one.

1954 — “wrong wall” arrives. QI’s Danville, Virginia citation flips the phrasing to reaching the top and discovering the ladder is leaning against the wrong wall, which is the shape the saying keeps from then on.

1980s — “of success” is added. Covey’s versions attach the ladder to success explicitly, in the 1986 Los Angeles Times report of his lectures and then in The 7 Habits. That addition is what makes the modern line quotable — and what makes it sound like his.
context.pull: Every retelling kept the ladder and moved the wall.
